prompt: A 128×64 monochrome display frame is 1,024 bytes. A full redraw takes about 23 ms over 400 kHz I2C but about 1 ms over 8 MHz SPI, counting payload only. What mainly explains the difference?

options.explanation: Neither bus compresses data; both send the same 1,024 bytes.

options.text: The SPI clock here is 20 times faster, and SPI does not spend a ninth acknowledgement clock on every byte
options.explanation: Correct. I2C uses nine clocks per byte and SPI eight, and 8 MHz is twenty times 400 kHz. Together those give roughly 23 ms against roughly 1 ms.

options.text: I2C needs two bits for every pixel
options.explanation: This display uses one bit per pixel on either bus. I2C's per-byte overhead is the acknowledgement clock.

options.text: SPI transfers happen in the background, so their time does not count
options.explanation: A blocking SPI call still takes about 1 ms. DMA can move the work off the CPU, but the transfer still takes time and needs scheduling.

workedExample:
1. Both buses send the same 1,024 payload bytes.
2. I2C spends nine clocks per byte (eight data bits plus ACK/NACK); SPI spends eight.
3. The example SPI clock is twenty times faster than 400 kHz I2C.
4. Addresses, commands and driver behaviour add time, so measure the real driver. Either way, a full redraw is too long to block inside a 1 ms audio callback.

link.title: A Basic Guide to I2C — Texas Instruments

prompt: A colleague updates a 128×64 OLED over 400 kHz I2C by calling a blocking `display.update()` at the end of the audio callback, to keep the screen "in sync". The audio block is 1 ms. What happens?

options.text: Nothing bad; I2C is handled by hardware
options.explanation: The peripheral clocks bits out, but a blocking call waits for the whole transfer, about 23 ms, inside the callback.

options.text: The audio callback overruns its 1 ms deadline by about 22 ms on every redraw, causing dropouts; move the display update to the main loop (or DMA)
options.explanation: Correct. Bus I/O that blocks for milliseconds must never run in the callback; the display can update at a relaxed rate from the foreground.

options.text: The display flickers but audio is unaffected
options.explanation: The callback cannot produce the next block while it is blocked, so audio is directly affected.

options.text: The I2C clock speeds up to keep pace
options.explanation: The bus speed is configured; it does not adapt to deadlines.

workedExample:
1. A blocking call waits for the whole transfer: about 23 ms for a full redraw at 400 kHz I2C.
2. The callback has 1 ms to produce each block, so each redraw makes it about 22 ms late and about 22 blocks are missed: audible dropouts.
3. Schedule display updates in the foreground at a modest rate, or use a suitable asynchronous/DMA driver.
4. Interrupt masking, memory-bus competition and driver behaviour still require measurement.

link.title: A Basic Guide to I2C — Texas Instruments

prompt: You are choosing buses for a synth with: DIN MIDI in, a codec with I2C control, a colour TFT display, and 32 extra LEDs. Which pairings are sensible? Select all that apply.

options.text: DIN MIDI on a hardware UART at 31,250 baud, through the spec's opto-isolated input circuit
options.explanation: Correct. MIDI over DIN is defined as an asynchronous serial interface at this rate.
Correct. A colour frame is far larger than a monochrome one; SPI's higher clock rates suit it.
I2C configures the codec; the sample stream needs the continuous, clocked I2S/SAI link.

options.text: LEDs through an I2C or SPI LED driver/expander chip
options.explanation: Correct. A driver chip saves pins and moves LED current off the MCU.

workedExample:
Match each job to the bus's strengths:

| Job | Bus |
|---|---|
| MIDI | UART |
| Codec control | I2C |
| Codec audio | I2S/SAI |
| TFT | SPI |
| LEDs | I2C/SPI driver |

The audio stream alone is large: 48 kHz stereo 24-bit audio carries about 2.3 million payload bits per second, far beyond Fast-mode I2C's 400 kbit/s. So I2C could not carry the stream even if it were designed for audio, which it is not.
